record.title: A survey of a literature-review agent reports stated trust despite mandatory checkpoints
record.summary: A preprint evaluates CoSLR, a multi-agent system for systematic literature reviews with retrieval grounding and mandatory human checkpoints. In a remote, self-paced survey study, 63 participants completed a simplified workflow in about 15 minutes; recruitment used convenience channels and participants were mainly from software engineering. The authors report that 22/63 (34.9%) rated their trust in generated summaries and reports at 4 or 5 on a five-point scale for acceptance without additional checking after brief interaction. They also report that 27/63 (42.9%) rated usability highly. These are post-interaction self-reports: the study did not observe full reviews or whether participants actually skipped verification.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a remote 15-minute, survey-based CoSLR evaluation with 63 convenience-recruited participants, 22/63 (34.9%) self-reported trust ratings of 4 or 5 for generated summaries and reports without additional checking after brief interaction. This measures stated willingness, not observed checkpoint use or actual unverified acceptance.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study does not establish observed checkpoint bypass, actual acceptance of unverified reports, or a causal effect of mandatory checkpoints.

evidence_gaps.description: The key trust measure is self-reported and the study did not observe complete reviews or actual verification behavior.
The 63-participant survey result has not been independently replicated in other disciplines or reviewer populations.

brief.importance_rationale: If similar attitudes occur in real review workflows, interfaces that rely on a mandatory checkpoint alone may not ensure evidence checking. The consequence is meaningful for research-integrity design, but evidence is a self-report from 63 convenience-recruited participants after a brief task and does not measure actual verification behavior.
limitations: The sample contains 63 voluntary convenience-recruited participants, primarily from software engineering backgrounds.
Participants completed a simplified, remote task in about 15 minutes; none completed a full systematic review.
The outcome is stated trust on a questionnaire, not observed verification or actual acceptance of unverified synthesis.
The paper reports author-run survey results; the research desk did not inspect participant-level data or independently reproduce the study.

technical.claimed_result: In a remote 15-minute, survey-based CoSLR evaluation with 63 convenience-recruited participants, 22/63 (34.9%) self-reported trust ratings of 4 or 5 for generated summaries and reports without additional checking after brief interaction. technical.demonstrated_result: The primary arXiv record and full-text methods/results establish that the authors report a 63-person questionnaire study and its self-reported answers; the research desk did not observe participant behavior or audit raw data.
technical.mechanism: CoSLR combines a multi-agent literature-review workflow with retrieval-augmented generation and mandatory human checkpoints. The study asks participants after a short interaction whether they would trust generated summaries and reports without additional checking.
technical.regime: Remote, self-paced simplified literature-review workflow, about 15 minutes per participant; N=63 convenience sample, primarily software-engineering students, researchers and professionals; 5-point questionnaire.
technical.strongest_baseline: No control group or matched manual-review condition. The bounded result is a descriptive self-report within CoSLR’s short system-use evaluation.

brief.title: A survey of a literature-review agent reports stated trust despite mandatory checkpoints
brief.why_it_matters: The study suggests that requiring a checkpoint may not ensure that users scrutinize AI-generated synthesis, even when they report the system is usable. Its bounded result is a self-reported attitude in a small convenience sample, not observed behavior or a causal estimate of checkpoint effectiveness.
